The Case Against the Insanity Defense: Why Mental Illness Should Not Excuse Criminal Responsibility

Introduction

For centuries, criminal law has recognized the concept that some defendants—those deemed "legally insane" at the time of their offense—should be partially or wholly excused from criminal punishment. The insanity defense, in its various formulations, rests on the premise that certain mental conditions render individuals incapable of forming the requisite criminal intent, or mens rea, that underpins our system of criminal justice. While this premise may appear compassionate on its surface, a careful examination reveals that the insanity defense is philosophically incoherent, practically unworkable, and ultimately destructive to the rule of law. It is time to abolish or, at the very least, severely restrict this defense.

This essay argues that the insanity defense should be eliminated from criminal jurisprudence—not because mental illness is unreal or unimportant, but because it functions as a mechanism by which dangerous individuals evade the consequences of their actions, undermines public confidence in justice, and rests on a fundamentally flawed understanding of both culpability and mental illness.

I. The Philosophical Failure: Free Will and the Myth of the "Responsible" Criminal

The insanity defense presupposes a binary distinction between the "responsible" and "irresponsible" offender—between those who freely chose to commit crime and those whose mental illness "made them do it." This distinction, upon close inspection, does not hold.

If we accept that severe mental illness negates moral responsibility, we must confront an uncomfortable question: what, precisely, makes any criminal "responsible"? Modern neuroscience and psychology have increasingly demonstrated that all human behavior—violent or otherwise—arises from the interplay of neurochemistry, genetic predisposition, early childhood experience, environmental stressors, and a host of other factors largely outside individual control. The sociopath who murders for pleasure has a disordered brain. The impoverished teenager who robs a convenience store has been shaped by deprivation and trauma. The addict who steals to fund a habit has been hijacked by neurochemical compulsions.

If the standard for criminal responsibility is "truly free choice unencumbered by mitigating psychological forces," then virtually no one qualifies. The insanity defense draws an arbitrary line through the spectrum of human motivation and declares those on one side morally blameless and those on the other fully culpable. This line is not grounded in any defensible moral philosophy; it is a legal fiction sustained by tradition, not reason.

The more honest and coherent approach is to acknowledge that criminal punishment serves purposes beyond the simple retribution for "free choices." It incapacitates dangerous individuals, deters harmful conduct, expresses society's moral condemnation of destructive acts, and protects the public. These purposes apply equally whether the offender committed murder due to paranoid schizophrenia, antisocial personality disorder, economic desperation, or simple greed.

II. The Empirical Failure: Mental Illness Does Not Eliminate Dangerousness

One of the central implicit claims of the insanity defense is that individuals who act under the influence of severe mental illness are fundamentally different from—and less dangerous than—those who act with "criminal intent." The empirical evidence strongly suggests otherwise.

Research consistently demonstrates that certain forms of mental illness, particularly when combined with substance abuse, are associated with increased rates of violent behavior. A landmark 2009 study published in The Lancet by Fazel and colleagues found that individuals with schizophrenia and related psychoses were approximately four to six times more likely to commit violent crimes than the general population. Substance abuse comorbidity amplified this risk substantially.

This does not mean that all mentally ill individuals are dangerous—far from it. But it means that those who do commit serious crimes while mentally ill pose genuine and significant risks to public safety. An insanity acquittal, followed by commitment to a psychiatric facility, has historically resulted in shorter periods of confinement than a criminal sentence would have imposed. Studies of insanity acquittees have found that many are released within years of their acquittal, sometimes after remarkably brief institutionalization.

The case of John Hinckley Jr.—who shot President Ronald Reagan in 1981 and was found not guilty by reason of insanity—illustrates this danger. Hinckley was eventually granted conditional release in 2016, and fully released in 2022, spending fewer years confined than many convicted armed robbers serve in prison. Whether one views Hinckley as a tragic figure or a dangerous one, the disparity between the severity of his act and the leniency of his confinement illustrates a systemic failure of the insanity framework to adequately protect the public.

Abolishing the insanity defense would not mean ignoring mental illness in the criminal process. Defendants could still raise mental health conditions as mitigating factors at sentencing, just as courts currently consider childhood abuse, economic hardship, and other background factors. But they would not be permitted to escape criminal conviction entirely, and sentencing judges—armed with psychiatric evaluations—could fashion proportionate sentences that account for both the seriousness of the offense and the defendant's mental health needs.

III. The Practical Failure: A Defense That Cannot Be Administered Fairly

Even setting aside the philosophical and empirical objections, the insanity defense fails on practical grounds. It is, bluntly, unworkable.

A. The Opacity of the Human Mind

The insanity defense requires judges and juries to determine what was happening inside a defendant's mind at the precise moment of a criminal act. This is an inherently impossible task. Psychiatric experts routinely disagree—often dramatically—about a defendant's mental state. The spectacle of dueling expert witnesses, with prosecution psychiatrists declaring a defendant perfectly sane and defense psychiatrists describing a shattered psyche, has become a cliché precisely because it reflects the reality of these proceedings.

Jurors, lacking any specialized training, are expected to weigh these competing assessments and render a verdict on a question that even the experts cannot agree upon. The result is that insanity verdicts are driven less by evidence than by the relative persuasiveness of expert witnesses, the charisma of attorneys, and the emotional reactions of jurors.

B. Cultural and Racial Bias

The application of the insanity defense is plagued by inequity. Research has consistently shown that defendants who are wealthy, white, and well-represented are far more likely to successfully mount an insanity defense than those who are poor, minority, or reliant on public defenders. The defense requires the resources to hire psychiatric experts, conduct extensive evaluations, and present complex psychological evidence—resources that are unavailable to most defendants.

This creates a two-tiered system of justice: one for the privileged few who can afford to prove their "insanity," and another for everyone else. A defense that can only be accessed by the wealthy is not a principle of justice; it is a mechanism of inequality.

C. Malingering and Manipulation

The insanity defense invites manipulation. Defendants have strong incentives to fabricate or exaggerate symptoms of mental illness, and even trained psychiatrists acknowledge the extraordinary difficulty of distinguishing genuine psychosis from sophisticated faking. The history of the insanity defense is littered with cases of successful malingering—individuals who convincingly performed insanity, escaped punishment, and were later revealed to have been entirely feigning their conditions.

Every dollar and hour spent investigating fraudulent insanity claims is a resource diverted from genuine mental health care for those who need it most.

IV. The Moral Injury: Denying Justice to Victims

Perhaps the most overlooked dimension of this debate is the impact of the insanity defense on crime victims and their families.

When a defendant is found not guilty by reason of insanity, the message delivered to victims is devastating: the person who harmed you has been declared not responsible for what was done to you. Your suffering was caused not by a criminal who chose to act, but by a "disease" that merely used a human body as its instrument. The moral universe in which your injury was a wrong—a violation that demands acknowledgment and consequence—is replaced by a clinical universe in which your injury was a symptom.

This is not merely a semantic distinction. It strikes at the heart of what victims need from the justice system: recognition that what happened to them was wrong, that the person who did it is morally accountable, and that society takes their suffering seriously. The insanity defense systematically denies victims all three of these needs.

Consider the family of a murder victim, sitting in a courtroom as a defense psychiatrist explains that the killer was in the grip of a psychotic delusion and therefore bears no criminal responsibility. Consider the victim of a violent assault, learning that their attacker has been declared "not guilty" and will be transferred not to prison but to a hospital. The insanity defense does not merely excuse the offender—it erases the crime, recasting it as a medical event rather than a moral one.

V. Addressing Counterarguments

A. "But mental illness is real and affects behavior."

Of course it does. No serious advocate for abolishing the insanity defense denies the reality of mental illness or its capacity to distort perception, impair judgment, and fuel destructive impulses. The argument is not that mental illness is irrelevant, but that it should not function as a complete excuse for criminal conduct.

Mental illness is already recognized at sentencing. Judges routinely impose reduced sentences, recommend treatment programs, and direct offenders to psychiatric facilities as part of their incarceration. Abolishing the insanity defense would not eliminate these practices; it would relocate them from the guilt phase to the sentencing phase, where they belong.

B. "Without the insanity defense, mentally ill defendants will be punished for something they couldn't control."

This objection proves too much. No defendant—sane or insane—fully "controls" the factors that shaped their behavior. Every criminal is the product of forces—biological, psychological, social—beyond their complete mastery. If the standard for criminal punishment requires total individual control over one's actions, then we must abolish the entire criminal justice system, not merely the insanity defense.

The more defensible position is that criminal punishment is justified not by the fiction of perfect free will, but by society's legitimate interest in condemning harmful conduct, protecting the public, and deterring future crime. These interests are served by holding mentally ill offenders criminally accountable, just as they are served by holding all other offenders accountable.

C. "Some mentally ill defendants genuinely cannot understand what they are doing."

This is the narrowest and most sympathetic version of the insanity defense—the claim that certain individuals, in the grip of profound psychosis, are so disconnected from reality that they literally cannot comprehend the nature or wrongfulness of their acts. Even if we accept this as true in a small number of cases, it does not justify the broad insanity defense as currently practiced.

Courts have historically applied the insanity defense far more expansively than this narrow scenario requires. The "irresistible impulse" test, for example, excuses defendants who knew their act was wrong but claimed they could not stop themselves—a standard so subjective and manipulable that it borders on absurdity. The Model Penal Code's formulation, adopted by many jurisdictions, excuses anyone who, "as a result of mental disease or defect," lacks "substantial capacity" to appreciate the criminality of their conduct or conform their behavior to the law—a standard broad enough to encompass a vast range of offenders.

If the concern is truly limited to the vanishingly small number of individuals who are so profoundly incapacitated that they genuinely cannot comprehend their own actions, a narrow statutory provision addressing competency—not a sweeping defense of "insanity"—would suffice. But the insanity defense as it exists today is not limited to this extreme case, and its practical operation cannot be confined to it.

VI. A Path Forward: Abolition with Compassionate Sentencing

Abolishing the insanity defense does not require callousness toward the mentally ill. It requires a reorganization of how the legal system addresses mental illness in criminal cases—moving the inquiry from the guilt phase to the sentencing phase, where it can be addressed more accurately, more fairly, and more consistently.

Under this framework:

  1. Guilt would be determined on the basis of conduct and intent, without the complicating overlay of psychiatric diagnoses and expert debates about "sanity."

  2. Mental health evidence would be fully admissible at sentencing, where judges could consider the full range of relevant factors—the defendant's psychiatric condition, the role of mental illness in the offense, the defendant's need for treatment, and the risk of future dangerousness—in crafting an appropriate sentence.

  3. Sentences could include mandatory treatment components, ensuring that mentally ill offenders receive psychiatric care as part of their criminal punishment rather than as an alternative to it.

  4. The public would be protected through criminal sentences that reflect the seriousness of the offense, with release contingent on demonstrated rehabilitation rather than psychiatric reassessment alone.

This approach has the virtue of honesty. It acknowledges that mental illness is a significant factor in many crimes without pretending that it transforms a criminal act into a non-criminal one. It delivers justice to victims by ensuring that those who harmed them are convicted of their crimes. And it protects the public by ensuring that dangerous individuals are confined for meaningful periods under the authority of criminal law.

Conclusion

The insanity defense is a relic of an era when the relationship between mind and behavior was poorly understood and when criminal law was searching for a mechanism to avoid punishing those it deemed morally blameless. We now know that the line between the "sane" and "insane" offender is far blurrier than our legal system pretends. We know that mentally ill offenders can be genuinely dangerous. We know that the defense is applied inequitably, manipulated by the cunning, and experienced as a profound injustice by victims.

It is time to retire the insanity defense and replace it with a system that takes mental illness seriously without using it as a license to escape accountability. The criminal law should convict those who commit harmful acts and then, at sentencing, address the full complexity of their circumstances—including mental illness—with the seriousness and nuance it deserves. Justice demands no less. And the public, which the law exists to serve, can accept nothing less.

Note: This essay presents one side of a genuine legal and philosophical debate. Many scholars, advocates, and legal professionals hold strong opposing views, arguing that the insanity defense serves essential moral and constitutional functions. A complete understanding of this issue requires engagement with those perspectives as well.

The insanity defense represents one of the most controversial aspects of modern criminal law, allowing defendants to escape criminal responsibility by claiming mental illness rendered them unable to understand their actions or distinguish right from wrong. While this defense emerged from well-intentioned efforts to ensure justice for the genuinely mentally incompetent, there are compelling reasons to either abolish or severely restrict its application in contemporary criminal proceedings.

The Problem of Accountability

Criminal law's fundamental purpose is to hold individuals accountable for their actions and protect society from harmful behavior. The insanity defense undermines this core principle by creating a categorical exemption that often fails to serve either justice or public safety. When defendants successfully invoke this defense, they may avoid meaningful consequences for serious crimes, sending a troubling message that mental illness can serve as a complete shield against responsibility.

This erosion of accountability is particularly problematic given that mental illness exists on a spectrum. Many individuals struggle with psychological conditions yet still maintain sufficient capacity to make moral choices and control their behavior. Creating broad exemptions risks excusing conduct that, while influenced by mental health issues, still represents a conscious decision to cause harm.

Protecting Public Safety

A reformed approach would better serve public safety by ensuring that dangerous individuals face appropriate consequences regardless of their mental state. Under current systems, those found not guilty by reason of insanity may be released once deemed no longer mentally ill, even if they remain prone to violence. This approach prioritizes the defendant's mental health status over the community's right to protection from dangerous individuals.

A system focused on criminal responsibility rather than mental state could ensure that those who commit serious crimes face imprisonment or other sanctions that genuinely protect society. Mental health treatment could still be provided within the correctional system without sacrificing public safety or the principles of justice.

Challenges in Implementation

The practical application of insanity defenses creates additional problems that support reform arguments. Determining someone's mental state at the time of an offense often relies on subjective expert testimony that can be manipulated or contradicted by competing psychological evaluations. This process transforms criminal trials into battles between mental health experts rather than examinations of evidence and facts.

Furthermore, wealthy defendants have significant advantages in mounting insanity defenses, as they can afford extensive psychological evaluations and expert witnesses. This creates a troubling disparity where justice depends more on financial resources than on the actual merits of mental health claims.

Alternative Approaches

Rather than eliminating all consideration of mental health in criminal proceedings, reformed systems could incorporate mental illness as a mitigating factor in sentencing while maintaining criminal responsibility. This approach would acknowledge the role of psychological conditions in criminal behavior without completely absolving defendants of accountability.

Courts could mandate treatment as part of sentences, ensuring that mental health needs are addressed while still imposing consequences for criminal acts. This balanced approach would serve both rehabilitative goals and public safety interests more effectively than the current binary system of guilty versus not guilty by reason of insanity.

Conclusion

The insanity defense, while historically significant, has outlived its usefulness in modern criminal justice systems. Reform or abolition would strengthen principles of personal responsibility, better protect public safety, and create more equitable treatment of defendants regardless of their financial circumstances. Mental illness undoubtedly affects human behavior, but it should inform how we treat and rehabilitate offenders rather than whether we hold them responsible for their actions.

A justice system that maintains accountability while providing appropriate treatment represents a more balanced and effective approach than one that allows complete exemption from criminal responsibility based on mental health status. Such reforms would better serve victims, communities, and even defendants themselves by ensuring that justice remains both compassionate and meaningful.

Abolishing—or, at the very least, severely restricting—the insanity defense is necessary to preserve the integrity, fairness, and public legitimacy of the criminal justice system. While compassion toward people with serious mental illness is morally important, the insanity defense as currently used too often functions as a procedural escape hatch: it can turn criminal responsibility into a contest over labels rather than an inquiry into the defendant’s actions and culpability. Criminal law is designed to address harmful conduct and protect society. When a defendant commits a crime, that harm is real and its consequences persist regardless of the individual’s psychiatric history. Mental illness may explain why someone acted, but explanation is not the same as justification. The legal system should not allow mental illness to nullify responsibility as a matter of doctrine.

Mental illness should not erase culpability

The fundamental purpose of criminal law is to determine whether a person is responsible for what they did and, if so, to impose consequences proportionate to the harm caused. The insanity defense rests on the idea that some mental states render a defendant incapable of understanding the wrongfulness of their actions or conforming their conduct to the law. Yet this framing blurs a vital distinction: a person can be mentally ill and still be morally and legally accountable. Most people with mental disorders are not violent criminals, and many mentally ill individuals understand rules, consequences, and social norms. The existence of mental illness, by itself, does not logically imply a lack of moral agency.

Furthermore, the insanity defense risks encouraging the troubling assumption that mental illness automatically destroys personal responsibility. That assumption is both empirically and philosophically unstable. Empirically, mental illness does not uniformly prevent people from discerning right and wrong. Philosophically, even when someone’s reasoning is distorted, they may still have agency in the sense relevant to criminal culpability: they acted intentionally, chose among options, or at least voluntarily engaged in conduct that foreseeably harmed others. Criminal responsibility does not require a person to be perfectly rational; it requires a legally meaningful level of blameworthiness, and severe mental illness does not automatically negate that level.

The insanity defense can undermine deterrence and public safety

A system that permits defendants to avoid conviction—or substantially reduce punishment—based on contested psychiatric testimony can weaken deterrence. Even when the legal outcomes are technically complex, the practical message to the public can be stark: “If you claim insanity and win, you might walk or receive a lesser outcome.” This perception matters because deterrence is partially informational; people must believe that crime carries consequences. When the insanity defense is broadly available or inconsistently applied, it can distort that message and increase the likelihood that offenders (or future offenders) treat criminal accountability as optional.

Public safety also suffers when the insanity defense creates uncertainty about responsibility and punishment. It is often argued that acquittal by reason of insanity leads to treatment. But that promise is not always realized. In reality, post-verdict outcomes can vary significantly: some individuals are released when their risk decreases, while others remain confined for long periods that may not correspond to the original harm. Both outcomes can be problematic. If the law aims to protect society, it should do so through predictable, enforceable mechanisms rather than by shifting criminal adjudication into uncertain psychiatric processes.

Psychiatric testimony is fallible and incentivized

The insanity defense depends heavily on expert evaluations, typically conducted after the fact, under adversarial conditions, and often without direct access to the defendant’s internal experience at the time of the crime. The brain is complex; psychiatric diagnoses are probabilistic; and assessments of “wrongfulness” or “ability to control conduct” are difficult to measure reliably. This opens the door to inconsistent results across courts and jurisdictions.

Moreover, the adversarial process can inadvertently incentivize “professional disagreement” as strategy. Defense attorneys may seek experts who interpret the facts in the defendant’s favor, while prosecutors may present contrasting experts. The jury is asked to decide between competing theories of mental state and culpability, often without adequate tools to judge which scientific account is more accurate. When the stakes involve life-altering freedom or confinement, a doctrine that relies so heavily on subjective interpretation is inherently vulnerable to error.

A criminal justice system should not allow liberty or accountability to hinge on controversial assessments that cannot be verified with the same rigor as objective facts.

Punishment and treatment serve different purposes

Critics of abolishing the insanity defense often reply that people with serious mental illness still need care and that the insanity plea allows that. That argument conflates two distinct questions: (1) whether a person is criminally responsible and (2) what interventions should be provided for safety and recovery.

Removing or limiting the insanity defense does not eliminate treatment. Courts can still order psychiatric evaluation, require medication compliance, mandate mental health services, and place individuals in specialized therapeutic settings where appropriate. The key difference is that treatment should not depend on exoneration. Mental health intervention can be a condition of sentencing or supervision rather than a substitute for accountability.

Indeed, it is often more ethically coherent to treat mental illness as a factor in sentencing and management, not a complete defense to culpability. A person can be held responsible for violent actions while still receiving the psychiatric care they need. By replacing insanity-based acquittal with risk-based and clinical decision-making during sentencing and corrections, the system can simultaneously enforce accountability and promote rehabilitation and safety.

“Not guilty by reason of insanity” invites moral and legal confusion

The insanity defense can suggest that some crimes are performed without agency and thus deserve no criminal condemnation. Yet the harm to victims remains the same, and condemnation is not merely punishment—it is the community’s moral judgment that wrongdoing is unacceptable. If mental illness automatically cancels criminal responsibility, victims may experience a second harm: the sense that the system disregarded their suffering or treated the event as a clinical accident rather than an intentional act with consequences.

A better approach is to maintain moral clarity while incorporating clinical nuance. Criminal law can recognize that mental illness can diminish culpability without erasing it entirely. Severe restriction of the insanity defense would prevent the most extreme outcomes—where defendants escape accountability altogether—while allowing individualized sentencing that reflects both the severity of the offense and the defendant’s treatment needs.

Alternatives exist that preserve fairness without excusing responsibility

Abolishing or severely restricting the insanity defense does not mean ignoring mental illness. Several workable alternatives can address the legitimate concerns behind the doctrine:

  1. Substantially limit eligibility. If the insanity defense remains at all, restrict it to narrow categories—such as cases involving profound inability to appreciate the nature of one’s conduct, with stringent evidentiary standards.
  2. Use mental illness as a sentencing factor rather than a complete bar. Courts can reduce sentences when mental illness meaningfully impairs judgment or impulse control, while still imposing accountability.
  3. Expand mental health courts and treatment-based sentencing. Divert some defendants to treatment programs when safety permits, but require at least a conviction or adjudicated responsibility.
  4. Ensure forensic evaluation and ongoing review in custody. Dangerousness assessments can guide confinement and treatment without requiring acquittal.

These approaches keep the focus where it belongs: on the defendant’s responsibility and the protection of the public, rather than on whether a jury can determine a contested psychiatric state under the insanity framework.

Conclusion

Mental illness is real, often devastating, and deserving of care. But moral compassion must not be confused with legal absolution. The insanity defense, particularly as broadly available and inconsistently applied, undermines criminal accountability, weakens public confidence, and relies on uncertain psychiatric judgments to determine whether victims’ harms will be met with real consequences. The criminal justice system can and should address mental illness through sentencing, treatment mandates, mental health supervision, and risk-based confinement where necessary—without granting mental illness a blanket power to negate responsibility. Abolishing or severely restricting the insanity defense is a decisive step toward a system that holds people accountable for the harm they cause while still recognizing the clinical realities that shape behavior.

Reforming the Insanity Defense: Accountability, Public Safety, and the Integrity of Criminal Justice

The insanity defense occupies one of the most controversial corners of criminal law. To many observers, it appears to offer a loophole through which defendants who committed serious crimes can avoid full responsibility. Although the defense is intended to serve justice in rare cases involving profound mental incapacity, its existence in broad or loosely applied form can undermine public confidence in the legal system, create inconsistency in verdicts, and obscure the central principle that criminal acts must carry consequences. For these reasons, the insanity defense should be severely restricted and replaced with a more rigorous framework that emphasizes accountability, public safety, and narrowly tailored consideration of genuine mental impairment.

At the heart of criminal justice is the idea that individuals are responsible for their actions. A legal system that too readily excuses criminal conduct because of psychiatric evidence risks weakening this principle. Mental illness exists on a spectrum, and many people who live with serious diagnoses still understand the difference between right and wrong, can control their behavior, and are fully capable of obeying the law. If mental illness is treated too readily as a basis for avoiding conviction, the law sends a confused message: that psychological difficulties can negate culpability even when a defendant planned a crime, understood its illegality, or attempted to conceal it. Such outcomes do not promote justice; they blur it.

Another serious problem is the uncertainty built into insanity determinations. Unlike many factual questions in a criminal trial, insanity depends heavily on expert testimony, retrospective interpretation, and competing psychiatric evaluations. Different experts may reach different conclusions about the same defendant, and juries are often asked to resolve highly technical disputes far outside ordinary experience. This creates a danger that verdicts will turn less on the underlying criminal act and more on which side presents a more persuasive expert. A justice system should not depend so heavily on subjective psychological assessments when deciding whether a person who undeniably committed a serious offense should be held criminally liable.

Broad use of the insanity defense also threatens public trust. When a defendant who committed a shocking or violent crime is found not guilty by reason of insanity, many citizens view the result as a denial of justice, especially when they believe the offender understood what he or she was doing. Even if such cases are statistically rare, they attract significant attention and shape public perception of the courts. A legal doctrine that repeatedly appears to separate wrongdoing from accountability can weaken confidence in institutions and fuel the belief that the system protects offenders more than victims. Criminal law must not only be fair; it must be seen as fair.

Severely restricting the insanity defense would not require ignoring mental illness altogether. Rather, mental illness should usually be considered at sentencing, in correctional treatment, and in post-conviction supervision—not as a complete bar to criminal responsibility. Under this approach, a defendant who commits a crime would still be convicted if the prosecution proves the elements of the offense, but courts could consider documented psychiatric impairment when determining punishment, treatment needs, institutional placement, or conditions of release. This would preserve the principle of accountability while still allowing individualized responses to genuine mental disorders.

A narrower rule would also better protect public safety. When defendants are acquitted on insanity grounds, they are often committed to psychiatric institutions, but the duration and conditions of confinement can become legally and administratively complicated. A system focused on conviction followed by secure treatment may produce clearer, more consistent outcomes. Defendants who pose a danger could be confined in forensic psychiatric facilities within the correctional system, ensuring both treatment and accountability. This model would reduce the perception that a person “got away with” a crime while still addressing mental health needs in a structured and secure setting.

Critics may argue that any severe restriction of the insanity defense is inhumane because some individuals truly cannot understand the nature or wrongfulness of their acts. That concern should be taken seriously. But even acknowledging such extreme cases does not justify a broad defense vulnerable to manipulation and inconsistent application. If a jurisdiction retains the defense at all, it should be limited to the rarest circumstances: only where a defendant, because of a severe and well-documented mental disorder, entirely lacked the capacity to understand the physical nature of the act or its wrongfulness. Anything less should not excuse criminal liability.

In addition, jurisdictions should adopt procedural safeguards to prevent misuse. The burden of proving insanity should rest on the defense and should require clear and convincing evidence. Mere diagnosis should never be enough. Evidence of planning, concealment, fleeing, or efforts to avoid detection should weigh heavily against the claim. Courts should also require independent expert evaluation rather than relying exclusively on hired experts. These reforms would preserve a narrow safety valve for exceptional cases while ensuring that the defense does not become a generalized escape from responsibility.
